# Monte Carlo Simulations

{{< include _mc-01-sample-estimator.qmd >}}



::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Example: Estimating the Mean from an i.i.d. Random Sample

Let
$$
\{X_1, \ldots, X_n\}
$$
be an i.i.d. random sample with $X_i \sim F_X$ for all $i = 1, \dots, n$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🤫 Psst … Secret Information

In this simulation, $F_X = \mathcal{N}(\mu_X, \sigma^2_X)$ with $\mu_X = 5$ and $\sigma^2_X = 10$. In practice, $F_X$, and thus $\mu_X$ and $\sigma^2_X$, are **unknown**.
:::

We estimate the unknown mean $\theta \equiv \mu_X$ by the **sample mean**
$$
\hat\theta_n \equiv \hat\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

The following code generates one realization of the random sample. The fixed seed, `set.seed(321)`, makes the pseudo-random numbers reproducible.

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(321)

mean_X <- 5
var_X  <- 10
n      <- 10

sample_X <- rnorm(n = n, mean = mean_X, sd = sqrt(var_X))
```

The observed realization, stored in `sample_X`,
$$
\{X_{1,\operatorname{obs}}, \ldots, X_{n,\operatorname{obs}}\} = \{`r round(sample_X[1], 2)`,\ `r round(sample_X[2], 2)`,\ \dots,\ `r round(sample_X[n], 2)`\}
$$
yields the estimate
$$
\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{i,\operatorname{obs}} = `r round(mean(sample_X), 2)`.
$$

A new sample yields a new estimate. The animation shows the observed sample (first frame, red) followed by further realizations of the random sample and of the estimator $\hat\theta_n$ (blue).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-retina: 1
#| fig.keep: !expr if (knitr::is_html_output()) "all" else "first"
#| animation.hook: !expr if (knitr::is_html_output()) "gifski" else NULL
#| interval: 1
R        <- 20                             # number of realizations
X_sample <- cbind(sample_X,                # first column: observed sample
                  matrix(rnorm(n * (R - 1), mean = mean_X, sd = sqrt(var_X)),
                         nrow = n))

for (r in seq_len(R)) {
  col_r <- if (r == 1) "darkred" else "steelblue"
  par(mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1, family = "serif", mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, n + 0.5), ylim = mean_X + c(-4, 4) * sqrt(var_X),
       xlab = "Observation i", ylab = expression(X[i]), xaxt = "n",
       main = if (r == 1) "Observed realization of the random sample"
              else paste0("Another realization (", r, " of ", R, ")"))
  axis(1, at = seq_len(n))
  abline(h = mean_X, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  abline(h = mean(X_sample[, r]), lwd = 2, col = col_r)
  points(seq_len(n), X_sample[, r], pch = 19, cex = 2, col = col_r)
  legend("topleft", bty = "n", lty = c(2, 1), lwd = c(1.5, 2),
         col = c(par("fg"), col_r), cex = 0.9,
         legend = c(bquote("true mean" ~ theta == .(mean_X)),
                    bquote("estimate" ~ hat(theta)[n] ==
                           .(format(round(mean(X_sample[, r]), 2), nsmall = 2)))))
}
```

**Summary:**

::: {.spaced-list}
* The data change from realization to realization, and so does the estimate. That is, $\hat\theta_n$ is a **random variable**, and $\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}}$ is just one of its realizations.

* The realizations of $\hat\theta_n$ lie close to the (usually unknown) true mean $\mu_X = 5$. That is, the distribution of $\hat\theta_n$ is **concentrated** around $\mu_X$. This concentration increases with the sample size $n$.
:::
:::



::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Example: Estimating Regression Coefficients from an i.i.d. Random Sample

Let
$$
\{(Y_1, X_1^\top), \ldots, (Y_n, X_n^\top)\}
$$
be an i.i.d. random sample with $(Y_i, X_i^\top) \sim F_{YX}$ for all $i = 1, \dots, n$, where

::: {.spaced-list}
* $Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + \varepsilon_i$ is the outcome, and

* $X_i \in \mathbb{R}^K$ is the vector of predictors of observation $i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🤫 Psst … Secret Information

In this simulation, $X_i = (1, X_{i2})^\top$ with $X_{i2} \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 4]$, $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ independent of $X_i$, and $\beta = (2, -1)^\top$. Together, these choices fully specify the joint distribution $F_{YX}$.

In practice, we assume (hopefully correctly) that we know the type of regression model, here the simple linear regression model
$$
Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + \varepsilon_i \quad\text{with}\quad X_i = (1, X_{i2})^\top.
$$

However, we know only the model's structure (here: an intercept and one predictor), not the entire model. In particular, we typically do **not know**:

::: {.spaced-list}
* the distribution of $X_i$,

* the distribution of $\varepsilon_i$, and

* the value of $\beta$.
:::

Thus, essential parts of $F_{YX}$, such as $\beta$, are **unknown**.
:::

We estimate the unknown coefficient vector $\theta \equiv \beta$ by the **OLS estimator**
$$
\hat\theta_n \equiv \hat\beta_n = \left(X^\top X\right)^{-1} X^\top Y,
$$
where
$$
X = \begin{pmatrix}
X_1^\top \\ X_2^\top \\ \vdots \\ X_n^\top
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
X_{11} & X_{12} & \cdots & X_{1K} \\
X_{21} & X_{22} & \cdots & X_{2K} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
X_{n1} & X_{n2} & \cdots & X_{nK}
\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
Y = \begin{pmatrix}
Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n
\end{pmatrix}
$$
are the $n \times K$ matrix of predictors and the $n \times 1$ vector of outcomes.

The following code generates one realization of the random sample and computes the estimate.

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(321)

n    <- 20
beta <- c(2, -1)

X   <- cbind(1, runif(n, min = 0, max = 4))   # first column: intercept
eps <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
Y   <- X %*% beta + eps

beta_hat <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% Y
```

The observed realization, stored in `Y` and `X`,
$$
\{(Y_{1,\operatorname{obs}}, X_{1,\operatorname{obs}}^\top), \ldots, (Y_{n,\operatorname{obs}}, X_{n,\operatorname{obs}}^\top)\} = \{(`r round(Y[1], 2)`,\ 1,\ `r round(X[1, 2], 2)`),\ \dots,\ (`r round(Y[n], 2)`,\ 1,\ `r round(X[n, 2], 2)`)\}
$$
yields the estimate, stored in `beta_hat`,
$$
\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}} = (`r round(beta_hat[1], 2)`,\ `r round(beta_hat[2], 2)`)^\top.
$$

A new sample yields a new estimate. The animation shows the observed sample (first frame, red) followed by further realizations of the random sample and of the estimator $\hat\theta_n$ (blue).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-retina: 1
#| fig.keep: !expr if (knitr::is_html_output()) "all" else "first"
#| animation.hook: !expr if (knitr::is_html_output()) "gifski" else NULL
#| interval: 1
R <- 20                                    # number of realizations

for (r in seq_len(R)) {
  if (r > 1) {                             # r = 1: observed sample
    X <- cbind(1, runif(n, min = 0, max = 4))
    Y <- X %*% beta + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  }
  b_r   <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% Y
  col_r <- if (r == 1) "darkred" else "steelblue"
  par(mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1, family = "serif", mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 4), ylim = c(-5, 5),
       xlab = expression(X[i2]), ylab = expression(Y[i]),
       main = if (r == 1) "Observed realization of the random sample"
              else paste0("Another realization (", r, " of ", R, ")"))
  abline(a = beta[1], b = beta[2], lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  abline(a = b_r[1], b = b_r[2], lwd = 2, col = col_r)
  points(X[, 2], Y, pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = col_r)
  legend("topright", bty = "n", lty = c(2, 1), lwd = c(1.5, 2),
         col = c(par("fg"), col_r), cex = 0.9,
         legend = c(bquote("true line:" ~ beta == group("(", list(.(beta[1]), .(beta[2])), ")")),
                    bquote("estimate:" ~ hat(beta)[n] ==
                           group("(", list(.(format(round(b_r[1], 2), nsmall = 2)),
                                           .(format(round(b_r[2], 2), nsmall = 2))), ")"))))
}
```

**Summary:**

::: {.spaced-list}
* The data change from realization to realization, and so does the estimate. That is, $\hat\theta_n$ is a **random vector**, and $\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}}$ is just one of its realizations.

* The estimated regression lines lie close to the (usually unknown) true line with $\beta = (2, -1)^\top$. That is, the distribution of $\hat\theta_n$ is **concentrated** around $\beta$. This concentration increases with the sample size $n$.
:::
:::

### Step 3: Write the Simulation Code

We implement the algorithm from above in three parts.

**(a) Set the design parameters.**

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(123)

mu    <- 1                             # true mean E(X)
sigma <- sqrt(2)                       # true standard deviation sd(X)
n_seq <- c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500)    # sample sizes
B     <- 10000                         # Monte Carlo replications
alpha <- 0.05                          # significance level
z     <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)          # standard normal quantile

## Random number generators for the two distributions F_X
r_FX <- list(
  "Normal"     = function(n) rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma),
  "Chi-square" = function(n) rchisq(n, df = 1)
)
```

**(b) Write a function for one replication.** It performs Steps 1 and 2 of the algorithm: it simulates one data set and returns the estimate and whether the confidence interval contains $\mu$.

```{r}
#| echo: true
one_replication <- function(n, r_X) {
  X_sim    <- r_X(n)                               # 1. simulate data
  mu_hat   <- mean(X_sim)                          # 2. compute estimate
  se_hat   <- sd(X_sim) / sqrt(n)                  #    and the CI
  CI_lower <- mu_hat - z * se_hat
  CI_upper <- mu_hat + z * se_hat
  covers   <- (CI_lower <= mu) & (mu <= CI_upper)
  c(mu_hat = mu_hat, covers = covers)
}
```

**(c) Repeat $B$ times for each design and compute the Monte Carlo approximations.**

```{r}
#| echo: true
results   <- data.frame()
estimates <- list()                                # keep realizations for plots

for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  for (n in n_seq) {
    sim <- replicate(B, one_replication(n = n, r_X = r_FX[[dist]]))
    mu_hat_B <- sim["mu_hat", ]                    # B realizations of the estimator
    covers_B <- sim["covers", ]                    # B coverage indicators (0/1)

    estimates[[paste(dist, n)]] <- mu_hat_B
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      dist     = dist,
      n        = n,
      Bias     = mean(mu_hat_B) - mu,
      Var      = mean((mu_hat_B - mean(mu_hat_B))^2),
      Var_theo = sigma^2 / n,
      MSE      = mean((mu_hat_B - mu)^2),
      Coverage = mean(covers_B)
    ))
  }
}
```


### Step 4: Present the Results

@tbl-mc-results reports the Monte Carlo approximations for all designs. @fig-mc-hist shows the simulated distributions of $\bar X_n$, and @fig-mc-mse-cov shows the MSE and the coverage probability as functions of $n$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-mc-results
#| tbl-cap: "Monte Carlo approximations ($B = 10{,}000$) for the sample mean. `Var (theory)` is the exact variance $\\sigma^2/n$. The nominal coverage is 0.95."
tab <- results
tab$Bias     <- sprintf("%.4f", tab$Bias)
tab$Var      <- sprintf("%.4f", tab$Var)
tab$Var_theo <- sprintf("%.4f", tab$Var_theo)
tab$MSE      <- sprintf("%.4f", tab$MSE)
tab$Coverage <- sprintf("%.3f", tab$Coverage)
names(tab)   <- c("$F_X$", "$n$", "Bias", "Var", "Var (theory)", "MSE", "Coverage")
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrrrrrr", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-mc-hist
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of the $B = 10{,}000$ realizations of $\\bar X_n$. The black curve is the normal approximation $\\mathcal{N}(\\mu, \\sigma^2/n)$ implied by the CLT; the dashed line marks $\\mu = 1$."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.5
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1, family = "serif",
    mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  for (n in c(5, 50)) {
    est  <- estimates[[paste(dist, n)]]
    xlim <- mu + c(-4, 4) * sigma / sqrt(n)
    hist(est[est > xlim[1] & est < xlim[2]], freq = FALSE,
         breaks = seq(xlim[1], xlim[2], length.out = 41),
         xlim = xlim, border = "white",
         col = if (dist == "Normal") "steelblue" else "darkred",
         main = bquote(F[X] == .(if (dist == "Normal") "N(1, 2)" else "Chi-square(1)") * "," ~ n == .(n)),
         xlab = expression(bar(X)[n]), ylab = "Density")
    curve(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma / sqrt(n)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
    abline(v = mu, lty = 2)
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-mc-mse-cov
#| fig-cap: "Left: MSE versus $n$ on log-log scales; the black line is the theoretical MSE $\\sigma^2/n$. Right: coverage probability versus $n$; the gray band shows the range $0.95 \\pm 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{0.95 \\cdot 0.05 / B}$ expected from Monte Carlo error alone."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mgp = c(3.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1, family = "serif",
    mar = c(4.5, 5, 1, 1))
cols <- c("Normal" = "steelblue", "Chi-square" = "darkred")
pchs <- c("Normal" = 19, "Chi-square" = 17)

## MSE
plot(NA, xlim = range(n_seq), ylim = range(results$MSE), log = "xy",
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "MSE (log scale)")
curve(sigma^2 / x, add = TRUE, lwd = 1.5)
for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  sub <- results[results$dist == dist, ]
  points(sub$n, sub$MSE, pch = pchs[dist], col = cols[dist], cex = 1.3)
}
legend("topright", bty = "n", pch = pchs, col = cols, legend = c("N(1, 2)", "Chi-square(1)"))

## Coverage
mc_se <- sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / B)
plot(NA, xlim = range(n_seq), ylim = c(0.7, 1), log = "x",
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "Coverage probability")
polygon(c(1, 1000, 1000, 1), 0.95 + c(-1, -1, 1, 1) * 1.96 * mc_se,
        col = "gray85", border = NA)
abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2)
for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  sub <- results[results$dist == dist, ]
  lines(sub$n, sub$Coverage, type = "b", pch = pchs[dist], col = cols[dist], lwd = 1.5)
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", pch = pchs, col = cols, lwd = 1.5,
       legend = c("N(1, 2)", "Chi-square(1)"))
```


### Step 5: Interpret the Results

```{r}
#| echo: false
cov_of <- function(d, n) sprintf("%.3f", results$Coverage[results$dist == d & results$n == n])
```

**Question 1: Bias, variance, and MSE.** The simulation confirms the theory (@tbl-mc-results and @fig-mc-mse-cov, left):

::: {.spaced-list}
* The bias is close to zero for all designs. The remaining deviations are of the order of the Monte Carlo standard error of the bias, $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)/B}$, e.g., $\sqrt{0.4/10{,}000} \approx 0.006$ for $n = 5$.

* The variance and the MSE match $\sigma^2/n$ and decrease at rate $1/n$, i.e., with slope $-1$ on log-log scales.

* Both distributions yield the same results, since these properties depend on $F_X$ only through $\sigma^2$.
:::

**Question 2: Coverage.** Here the simulation reveals what asymptotic theory cannot (@tbl-mc-results and @fig-mc-mse-cov, right):

::: {.spaced-list}
* **Under-coverage for small $n$:** For $n = 5$, the coverage is only `r cov_of("Normal", 5)` (normal) and `r cov_of("Chi-square", 5)` ($\chi^2_1$) instead of $0.95$. Even for normal data, the interval is too short because it ignores the estimation uncertainty in $s_n$. (Using the $t_{n-1}$-quantile instead of $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ would fix this for normal data, but not for skewed data.)

* **The shape of $F_X$ matters:** Under the skewed $\chi^2_1$ distribution, the convergence to $0.95$ is much slower. Even for $n = 100$, the coverage is `r cov_of("Chi-square", 100)`. The reason is visible in @fig-mc-hist: for small $n$, the distribution of $\bar X_n$ is still skewed, so the normal approximation behind the interval is poor.

* **Large $n$:** For $n = 500$, the coverage is close to $0.95$ in both cases, as the CLT predicts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## How Precise Are the Monte Carlo Results?

Monte Carlo approximations are themselves estimates based on $B$ replications. For a coverage probability $p$, the **Monte Carlo standard error** is
$$
\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{B}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{0.95 \cdot 0.05}{10{,}000}} \approx 0.002.
$$
Thus, deviations from $0.95$ within about $\pm 0.004$ (the gray band in @fig-mc-mse-cov) can be pure Monte Carlo error, while the under-coverage found above is real. To halve the Monte Carlo error, quadruple $B$.
:::

## Simulation Example: Hypothesis Testing

We now apply the blueprint to a hypothesis test about $\mu$, using the same design as above: $F_X \in \{\mathcal{N}(1, 2), \chi^2_1\}$, $\sigma^2 = 2$, and $B = 10{,}000$.


<!-- Consistency section: commented out (redundant with the bias/variance simulations)

### Consistency

**Question.** By the definition of consistency above, the sample mean is consistent if
$$
P\left(\left|\bar X_n - \mu\right| \leq \varepsilon\right) \to 1 \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty
$$
for any $\varepsilon > 0$. How fast does this probability approach $1$, and how does the speed depend on $\varepsilon$?

**Code.** No new simulation is needed: we reuse the $B$ realizations of $\bar X_n$ stored in `estimates` and compute the Monte Carlo approximation
$$
\widehat{P}_{\operatorname{MC}}\left(\left|\bar X_n - \mu\right| \leq \varepsilon\right) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\left(\left|\hat\mu_{n,b} - \mu\right| \leq \varepsilon\right)
$$
for a grid of $\varepsilon$ values.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
eps_seq <- seq(0, 1.5, by = 0.01)              # grid of epsilon values
n_plot  <- c(5, 20, 100, 500)                   # sample sizes to compare

prob_close <- function(mu_hat_B, eps) {
  mean(abs(mu_hat_B - mu) <= eps)
}

## One curve per distribution and sample size
prob_curves <- list()
for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  for (n in n_plot) {
    mu_hat_B <- estimates[[paste(dist, n)]]
    prob_curves[[paste(dist, n)]] <- sapply(eps_seq, prob_close, mu_hat_B = mu_hat_B)
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-mc-consistency
#| fig-cap: "Monte Carlo approximations of $P(|\\bar X_n - \\mu| \\leq \\varepsilon)$ as functions of $\\varepsilon$. As $n$ grows, the curves approach $1$ for every $\\varepsilon > 0$."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1, family = "serif",
    mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
n_cols <- hcl.colors(length(n_plot) + 1, "Blues 3")[seq_along(n_plot)]
n_cols <- rev(n_cols)
for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  plot(NA, xlim = range(eps_seq), ylim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = expression(epsilon),
       ylab = expression(P(group("|", bar(X)[n] - mu, "|") <= epsilon)),
       main = if (dist == "Normal") "N(1, 2)" else "Chi-square(1)")
  for (k in seq_along(n_plot)) {
    lines(eps_seq, prob_curves[[paste(dist, n_plot[k])]], lwd = 2, col = n_cols[k])
  }
  abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
  legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = n_cols,
         legend = paste("n =", n_plot))
}
```

**Interpretation** (@fig-mc-consistency):

::: {.spaced-list}
* For every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, the probability increases towards $1$ as $n$ grows. This is consistency.

* The smaller $\varepsilon$, the larger the sample size needed to get close to $1$. Consistency says only that the probability converges, not how fast.

* Both distributions behave very similarly. For the sample mean, consistency depends on $F_X$ essentially only through $\sigma^2$.
:::
-->


### Step 1: Define the Test and the Questions

Consider the test of
$$
H_0\colon \mu = \mu_0 \quad\text{against}\quad H_1\colon \mu \neq \mu_0
$$
based on the $t$-statistic
$$
T_n = \frac{\sqrt{n}\left(\bar X_n - \mu_0\right)}{s_n}.
$$
We reject $H_0$ if $|T_n| > z_{1-\alpha/2}$. By the CLT, as $n \to \infty$,

::: {.spaced-list}
* the **size**, i.e., the rejection probability if $H_0$ is true, converges to $\alpha$, and

* the **power**, i.e., the rejection probability if $H_0$ is false, converges to $1$.
:::

How large are size and power for small $n$?

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Tests and Confidence Intervals

We reject $H_0\colon \mu = \mu_0$ if and only if $\mu_0 \notin \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n$. Thus, under $H_0$,
$$
P\left(\text{reject } H_0\right) = 1 - P\left(\mu_0 \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right),
$$
i.e., the size is one minus the coverage probability. The under-coverage found above therefore implies that the test rejects a true $H_0$ too often.
:::


### Step 2: Choose the Simulation Design

We test $\mu_0 = 1$ and vary the **true** mean $\mu$ over a grid from $0$ to $2$. To shift the mean without changing the shape of $F_X$, we generate
$$
X_i = \mu + U_i,
$$
where $U_i$ has mean zero and variance $2$: either $U_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2)$ or $U_i \sim \chi^2_1 - 1$. We consider $n \in \{20, 100\}$.


### Step 3: Write the Simulation Code

As before, we write a function for one replication and repeat it $B$ times for each design.

```{r}
#| echo: true
mu_0    <- 1                                    # hypothesized mean
mu_grid <- seq(0, 2, by = 0.1)                  # true means
n_test  <- c(20, 100)                           # sample sizes

## Random number generators for the mean-zero errors U
r_U <- list(
  "Normal"     = function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma),
  "Chi-square" = function(n) rchisq(n, df = 1) - 1
)

one_test <- function(n, mu_true, r_U_dist) {
  X_sim  <- mu_true + r_U_dist(n)                         # 1. simulate data
  T_stat <- sqrt(n) * (mean(X_sim) - mu_0) / sd(X_sim)   # 2. test statistic
  abs(T_stat) > z                                         #    reject H0?
}

test_results <- data.frame()
for (dist in names(r_U)) {
  for (n in n_test) {
    for (mu_true in mu_grid) {
      reject_B <- replicate(B, one_test(n = n, mu_true = mu_true,
                                        r_U_dist = r_U[[dist]]))
      test_results <- rbind(test_results, data.frame(
        dist = dist, n = n, mu = mu_true,
        Reject = mean(reject_B)                 # MC rejection probability
      ))
    }
  }
}
```

### Steps 4 and 5: Present and Interpret the Results

@fig-mc-power shows the rejection probabilities as functions of the true mean $\mu$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-mc-power
#| fig-cap: "Monte Carlo rejection probabilities of the $t$-test of $H_0\\colon \\mu = 1$ as functions of the true mean $\\mu$. At $\\mu = 1$ (dotted line), the curves show the size; elsewhere, they show the power. The dashed line marks $\\alpha = 0.05$."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1, family = "serif",
    mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (n in n_test) {
  plot(NA, xlim = range(mu_grid), ylim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = expression("True mean " * mu), ylab = "Rejection probability",
       main = paste("n =", n))
  abline(h = alpha, lty = 2)
  abline(v = mu_0, lty = 3)
  for (dist in names(r_U)) {
    sub <- test_results[test_results$dist == dist & test_results$n == n, ]
    lines(sub$mu, sub$Reject, type = "b", pch = pchs[dist], col = cols[dist], lwd = 1.5)
  }
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = pchs, col = cols, lwd = 1.5, cex = 0.85,
         legend = c("N(1, 2)", "Chi-square(1)"))
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
rej_of <- function(d, n, mu_val) {
  sprintf("%.3f", test_results$Reject[test_results$dist == d & test_results$n == n &
                                      abs(test_results$mu - mu_val) < 1e-8])
}
```

::: {.spaced-list}
* **Size:** At $\mu = \mu_0$, the rejection probability for $n = 20$ is `r rej_of("Normal", 20, 1)` (normal) and `r rej_of("Chi-square", 20, 1)` ($\chi^2_1$) instead of $\alpha = 0.05$. As expected, this is approximately one minus the coverage probabilities in @tbl-mc-results; the small differences are Monte Carlo error.

* **Power:** The further $\mu$ is from $\mu_0$, the higher the power. For $n = 100$, the power is close to $1$ already for $|\mu - \mu_0| \geq 0.6$; for $n = 20$, a much larger distance is needed.

* **Skewness:** Under $\chi^2_1$, the power curve is **asymmetric**. For $n = 20$ and $\mu = 1.3$, the power (`r rej_of("Chi-square", 20, 1.3)`) is even smaller than the size. Again, the normal approximation is poor for skewed data and small $n$.
:::
